Wellpleasing
wel-plēz'ing
adj. (acceptable, giving satisfaction; of sacrifices and of obedience that God receives)
The Authorized Version's compound for Greek euarestos — from eu (well) and arestos (pleasing). The related verb is used of Enoch, who before his translation had this testimony, that he pleased God.

Biblical Definition

Paul uses the word of a gift sent to him in prison by a poor church: “But I have all, and abound: I am full, having received of Epaphroditus the things which were sent from you, an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, wellpleasing to God” (Philippians 4:18). The vocabulary is the vocabulary of the altar — a sweet savour, a sacrifice — applied to money given to support a preacher. Hebrews then uses it in the great benediction: the God of peace “Make you perfect in every good work to do his will, working in you that which is wellpleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ” (Hebrews 13:21). Two things in that sentence prevent any doctrine of self-improvement. God is the one working in you, and the acceptance is through Jesus Christ. Whatever is wellpleasing in the believer, God Himself produced it and Christ presents it. Paul draws the same conclusion for the whole of life: “that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service” (Romans 12:1). The believer's ordinary obedience is not a lesser thing than the temple offerings; it is what those offerings pointed toward.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines well-pleasing as pleasing in a high degree, acceptable, and acceptable as pleasing or agreeable to a receiver.

expand to see more

WELL-PLEASING, a. Pleasing in a high degree; acceptable.

ACCEPTABLE, a. That may be received with pleasure; hence pleasing to a receiver; gratifying.

SAVOR, n. Taste or odor; something that perceptibly affects the organs of taste and smell.

SACRIFICE, n. An offering made to God on an altar, by means of a regular liturgy.

2. Destruction, surrender or loss made or incurred for gaining some object.

Key Scripture

Philippians 4:18 — "But I have all, and abound: I am full, having received of Epaphroditus the things which were sent from you, an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, wellpleasing to God."

Hebrews 13:21 — "Make you perfect in every good work to do his will, working in you that which is wellpleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ; to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen."

Romans 12:1 — "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service."

Hebrews 13:20 — "Now the God of peace, that brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the everlasting covenant,"

Modern Corruption

Pleasing God is turned into a transaction that earns His favour, or dismissed altogether as though grace made obedience irrelevant.

expand to see more

The idea that a Christian may do what is wellpleasing to God has been made to carry a weight it cannot bear, as though the believer's acceptance rose and fell with his performance. Hebrews 13:21 rules that out in its own clause structure: the good work is God working in us, and its acceptability is through Jesus Christ. The Father is not weighing the offering on its own merits. He receives it in the Son, which is why a small gift from a poor congregation at Philippi could be called a sacrifice of a sweet smell. Justified men please God; they do not procure their justification by pleasing Him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word. The principle to recover is that God is genuinely pleased with the obedience of His children. A reaction against merit-theology has produced preaching in which nothing the believer does matters at all, and the effect is to leave Christians with no motive but gratitude in the abstract and no sense that the Father delights in a son's obedience. Scripture is warmer than that. Enoch had this testimony, that he pleased God; the Philippians' gift was a sweet savour; and the words well done are spoken at the end to servants whose faithfulness was itself the gift of grace.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek euarestos (G2101), wellpleasing — Philippians 4:18, Hebrews 13:21, Romans 12:1-2; the verb euaresteo (G2100) — Hebrews 11:5-6.

expand to see more

Greek euarestos (G2101) — wellpleasing, acceptable; Romans 12:1, Philippians 4:18, Hebrews 13:21, Colossians 3:20.

Greek euaresteo (G2100) — to please well; Hebrews 11:5 of Enoch, and Hebrews 11:6, that without faith it is impossible to please him.

Greek osme euodias — an odour of a sweet smell; Philippians 4:18, the language of Leviticus applied to a church's gift.

Greek katartizo (G2675) — to make complete, to mend; Hebrews 13:21, rendered make you perfect.

Hebrews 11:6 sets the condition: without faith it is impossible to please him.

Usage

"“A sacrifice acceptable, wellpleasing to God” — said of money sent to a prisoner."

"“Working in you that which is wellpleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ” — God works it, Christ presents it."

"Justified men please God; they do not buy their justification with it."
